title: Claude Code 101
brief: A single-session course on Claude Code, built on one project. Nine chapters in an order where each one fixes the problem the last one created: what it is, installing, the loop it runs, a first prompt that goes wrong, the memory file that fixes it, the explore-plan-code-commit workflow, long sessions, MCP, and hooks. Cut as bone chapter cards with a running spine against full-frame session windows, an editor and wiring diagrams.
angle: Almost every bad session comes from the same thing: it did not know where it was, and nobody had told it.

segments.prompt: Cold open on the end state: a long session that shipped a feature, then pull back

events.note: one instruction, eleven minutes ago

lines: Explore upload paths · 6 tool uses · 61.2k tokens
Explore the test setup · 3 tool uses
2. A JPEG upload is saved as .webp

4. Replacing an avatar deletes the old one

events.text: Bash(git commit -m 'Add avatar upload with webp conversion')

beats.heading: Start at the end
beats.narration: Before anything else, look at where this ends up. One session, sixty-one turns deep, eleven minutes old, and still doing exactly what it was asked to do.

beats.heading: One instruction
beats.narration: It got one instruction. Ship a feature, write the tests, commit it. Not a conversation, not forty corrections. One sentence, and then it went to work.

beats.heading: It read first
beats.narration: It read before it wrote. Three agents, sixty thousand tokens of your codebase, working out how uploads already happen here. That reading is why the rest of this worked.

beats.heading: It wrote a contract
beats.narration: Then it wrote down how you would know it had succeeded. Four checks, each one something you can actually run. That list is the difference between a plan and a wish.

beats.heading: It asked
beats.narration: And it asked before touching anything. Four files, sixty-three lines. You get to see the size of the change before you agree to it.

beats.heading: It checked itself
beats.narration: It ran the tests itself and reported them against the list it wrote earlier. Four of four green, and it did not need to be asked twice.

beats.heading: It committed
beats.narration: Then a commit with a message that says what it did. That is the whole loop, and none of it was luck.

beats.heading: The catch
beats.narration: Here is the catch. Type that same sentence into a fresh install today and it goes badly. Everything that made this work happened before it. That is what the next half hour is.

segments.prompt: The video title

titlecard.note: Nine things, in the order they stop hurting

beats.heading: The whole course
beats.narration: This is the whole thing in one sitting. Nine parts, one project, and each part fixes the problem the one before it created.

beats.heading: How to watch
beats.narration: You do not need to take notes. You need to watch the order.

segments.prompt: Chapter one card: what Claude Code actually is

waypoint.promise: You will know why this is not autocomplete

beats.heading: Chapter one
beats.narration: Start with what the thing actually is, because almost everyone arrives with the wrong picture of it in their head.

beats.heading: The wrong picture
beats.narration: The wrong picture is a smarter autocomplete. Get that wrong and every habit you build on top of it is wrong too.

segments.prompt: What it is: an agent with tools that reads and edits your actual repo

events.text: why does the login route return 500 on a bad password?

events.note: it goes looking, not guessing

events.text: A thrown Error becomes a 500. This wants a 401.
lines: The handler has no catch, so Express falls through to the default.

beats.heading: A real question
beats.narration: Here is the same tool three turns into a real project, being asked a question you would actually ask a colleague on your team.

beats.heading: Not a code request
beats.narration: Notice what the question is not. It is not write me a function. It is a why question about behaviour, and answering it means going and looking.

beats.heading: It searches
beats.narration: So it searches. This is the first thing that separates it from autocomplete, which has only ever seen the file you have open and the lines just above your cursor.

beats.heading: It reads
beats.narration: Then it opens the file it found and reads it. A hundred and twenty four lines, and it comes back pointing at line sixty one.

beats.heading: It reasons
beats.narration: And it explains the mechanism rather than the symptom. A thrown error with no catch becomes a five hundred, and this case wants a four oh one.

beats.heading: It edits
beats.narration: Then it edits the file. Not a suggestion in a side panel you copy out. The file on your disk, in your repo, that your tests run against.

beats.heading: It runs it
beats.narration: And it runs your test suite to check its own work. Search, read, reason, edit, run. Those five verbs are what the word agent means here.

beats.heading: The shape of it
beats.narration: One question, five tools, a real fix. That is the shape of every session you will ever have with it.

segments.prompt: Breath: it has tools, and that changes what you should ask for

titlecard.note: So ask for outcomes, not lines of code

beats.heading: The real difference
beats.narration: The difference is not that the model is cleverer. It is that this one can act. It reads, edits, and runs things.

beats.heading: What to ask for
beats.narration: Which means you stop asking for code and start asking for outcomes.

waypoint.promise: Running, signed in, and pointed at a real project

beats.heading: Chapter two
beats.narration: Getting it running takes about two minutes, and there is exactly one decision in it worth thinking about.

beats.heading: The one decision
beats.narration: That decision is which directory you start it in, and it matters more than anything else on this screen.

segments.prompt: Install: npm install, launch, auth, the welcome box, and where you started it

events.note: node 18 or newer

aside: Run /init to create a CLAUDE.md file
events.note: the directory is the working set

lines: /init      write a CLAUDE.md for this project

beats.heading: One install line
beats.narration: It is one global npm install and a terminal. There is no project setup, no config file to write first, and nothing you add to your repository. It is a tool on your machine, not a dependency of your code.

beats.heading: The install
beats.narration: One package, four seconds. You need Node eighteen or newer, and that is the entire dependency list. There is a native installer as well if you would rather not go through npm at all.

beats.heading: Then log in
beats.narration: Then you run claude, and the first launch walks you through signing in. That happens in the browser once and is remembered afterwards, so every launch after this one drops you straight at the prompt.

beats.heading: The one decision
beats.narration: And here is that one decision. The directory you launched from is the directory it can see. Start it in your home folder and it is looking at everything and understanding nothing. Launch it from the root of one repository, the one you actually want help with.

beats.heading: Slash help
beats.narration: Slash help is the map. Everything in this video that starts with a slash is on that list, the list is short enough to read in a minute, and it is worth doing once on your first day.

beats.heading: Four of them
beats.narration: Four of these matter today, and three of them are for problems you have not hit yet. Init writes the memory file. Compact buys back room. Rewind undoes work rather than words. We will hit all three.

beats.heading: Ready
beats.narration: Installed, signed in, pointed at one project. Now the part worth understanding.

segments.prompt: Chapter three card: how it works

waypoint.promise: The loop it runs, and the one budget that governs everything

beats.heading: Chapter three
beats.narration: This is the chapter that makes the other six make sense, so it is worth three minutes of your attention.

beats.heading: Two things
beats.narration: Two things to take from it. The loop it runs in, and the single budget that every problem later in this video comes back to.

segments.prompt: The loop: your prompt, it reads, it proposes, you approve, round again

nodes.label: It reads
nodes.note: the files it decides are relevant

nodes.label: It proposes
nodes.note: edits, with a reason for each

nodes.label: You approve
nodes.note: nothing touches disk until you do

beats.heading: Five parts
beats.narration: Every session is this loop, over and over. Five parts, four hops between them, and one arc that takes you back to the beginning. Learn this and the rest of the video is detail.

beats.heading: You ask
beats.narration: It starts with your instruction as plain text. No syntax, no template, no special vocabulary to learn. The quality of everything downstream is set right here, which is why chapter four is entirely about this one step and nothing else.

beats.heading: It reads
beats.narration: Then it decides what to look at and goes and looks. Searches, file reads, sometimes running a command just to see what it prints. It is building a picture of your project from scratch, every session, and it is spending real budget to do it.

beats.heading: It proposes
beats.narration: Out of that reading comes a proposal, and it arrives as a diff. Lines out, lines in, with a reason attached to each change. At this point it is a suggestion and nothing more, which is worth remembering when it proposes something alarming.

beats.heading: You approve
beats.narration: Nothing reaches your disk until you agree to it. That gate is the single most important control you have in this whole tool, and in chapter six you will see exactly what each of the answers to it hands over.

beats.heading: Round again
beats.narration: Then it comes back round with whatever you say next, carrying everything from the lap before it. That accumulation is the entire reason this tool is good at hour two, and also the entire reason it starts to struggle at hour three.

beats.heading: The whole loop
beats.narration: Ask, read, propose, approve, round again. Nine times out of ten, when a session goes wrong, one of those five is being skipped.

segments.prompt: The context window: the budget that governs everything, and what fills it

events.note: every read costs budget

events.text: Context is filling. Older turns will be summarised soon.

beats.heading: One number
beats.narration: There is one number that governs almost everything about working with this tool, and it has been sitting quietly in the corner of the screen this whole time.

beats.heading: It costs to read
beats.narration: Everything it knows about your project, it knows because it read it during this session. And every read costs a piece of a fixed budget called the context window.

beats.heading: A big file
beats.narration: One fourteen hundred line file is a meaningful slice of that budget. Read six of them and most of your session has gone on looking rather than doing, which is how an afternoon disappears.

beats.heading: What happens at the top
beats.narration: When it fills up, the oldest part of the conversation gets summarised away to make room. Which means a long session quietly forgets its own beginning, including the instructions you gave it at the start.

beats.heading: Watch it
beats.narration: So watch that number. It is the difference between a session that gets better for an hour and one that gets steadily worse while sounding just as confident.

beats.heading: Remember this
beats.narration: Hold on to that. Chapters five and seven are both answers to this one problem.

segments.prompt: Chapter four card: your first prompt, and how it goes wrong

waypoint.promise: You will see exactly how a reasonable request goes wrong

beats.heading: Chapter four
beats.narration: Now we give it something real to do, on a project it has never seen, with no preparation at all.

beats.heading: It goes wrong
beats.narration: It goes wrong. Watch it carefully, because the next five chapters exist to fix precisely what happens here.

segments.prompt: A reasonable first prompt on a fresh project, and the four wrong guesses it makes

events.text: add a rate limiter to the login route
events.note: a fair request, badly under-specified
this project uses pnpm
middleware lives in src/http/ here
two lockfiles now disagree

events.text: Login is now limited to five attempts a minute.
lines: The failing tests look like an environment issue.

beats.heading: Turn one
beats.narration: Fresh project, turn one, nothing configured. This is the state almost everybody is in the first time they try this, and it is worth watching what that costs.

beats.heading: A fair request
beats.narration: The request is completely reasonable. Add a rate limiter to the login route. If you said that to a new engineer on your team, they would know what to do.

beats.heading: Wrong package manager
beats.narration: First guess. It reaches for npm, because npm is what most projects use. This project uses pnpm, and it has just written a second lockfile into your repository.

beats.heading: Wrong directory
beats.narration: Second guess. It creates a middleware folder, because that is where most projects keep middleware. In this project middleware lives under source, http. Now the repository has two conventions for the same thing.

beats.heading: The code is fine
beats.narration: And notice the code itself is fine. That is the uncomfortable part of this chapter. Every one of these guesses is defensible in isolation, and the result is still something you would send back in review.

beats.heading: The tests fail
beats.narration: Third guess. It runs the test suite with npm, on a project installed with pnpm, and three tests fail because the module it installed is not where this project looks for modules.

beats.heading: Confidently done
beats.narration: Fourth and worst. It reports success and waves the failures away as an environment problem. It is not lying to you. It genuinely has no way to know what this project's environment is.

beats.heading: Whose fault
beats.narration: This is the moment most people decide the tool is not ready. It is the wrong conclusion. Nothing here was a reasoning failure. It was four missing facts.

segments.prompt: Breath: it guessed, and every guess was reasonable

titlecard.note: Four times, and every guess was reasonable

beats.heading: Not stupidity
beats.narration: Every wrong answer there came from a missing fact, not from bad reasoning. It guessed because nobody had told it.

beats.heading: So tell it
beats.narration: Which means the fix is not a cleverer prompt. The fix is writing the facts down once.

segments.prompt: Chapter five card: the memory file

waypoint.promise: The four facts it guessed at, written down once

beats.heading: Chapter five
beats.narration: So we write the facts down. One file, committed to the repository, loaded into every session automatically.

beats.heading: Four facts
beats.narration: Specifically the four it just got wrong. This chapter is the direct answer to the last one.

segments.prompt: Slash init writes the first draft by reading the project

lines: Found: Express, pnpm, vitest, src/http/ middleware
events.note: it can find these facts itself

beats.heading: Not by hand
beats.narration: You do not write this file by hand on a blank page. There is a command whose entire job is to write the first draft of it for you.

beats.heading: Slash init
beats.narration: Slash init. You run it once, in the root of the project, on the day you start working there. It is the only setup step this tool has.

beats.heading: It finds them
beats.narration: And look at what it finds. The lockfile tells it pnpm. The test config tells it vitest. Eighteen files tell it where middleware lives. Every fact it guessed at in the last chapter was discoverable.

beats.heading: A draft
beats.narration: Twenty-six lines, written in about a minute. Treat it as a draft, because the version that earns its place is the one you cut down afterwards.

beats.heading: Now edit it
beats.narration: So let us look at what a good one actually contains, because the draft it just wrote is longer than it needs to be.

segments.prompt: The file itself: what belongs in it, section by section

lines: An Express API for task management. TypeScript, pnpm, vitest.
SQLite in development, Postgres in production.
blocks.note: one or two sentences, no more
this is the pnpm guess, fixed

lines: - Routes in `src/routes/`, one file per resource
- Services hold the logic, routes stay thin
blocks.note: and this is the directory guess, fixed

lines: - Errors return a status, never throw to the handler
Run `pnpm test` before saying a task is done.
blocks.note: the rules that keep getting broken

beats.heading: The whole file
beats.narration: This is a good one, and the first thing to notice is how short it is. Five sections, about twenty lines. Every line of it is loaded into every session, so every line has to earn the space.

beats.heading: At the root
beats.narration: It sits at the root of the repository and it gets committed. That is what makes it a team artifact rather than a personal setting. Your whole team gets the same memory.

beats.heading: What this is
beats.narration: First, what the project is, in two sentences. Stack, database, nothing more. This is the part it cannot reliably work out in one pass, and getting it wrong colours everything else.

beats.heading: The commands
beats.narration: Then the commands, and here is the first guess from chapter four being paid off. Install with pnpm. Test with pnpm. It will never reach for npm in this project again.

beats.heading: The layout
beats.narration: Then the layout, which pays off the second guess. Middleware goes in http, not middleware. One line, and the wrong directory stops happening forever.

beats.heading: House rules
beats.narration: Then your house rules. Named exports. Errors return a status rather than throwing. That second one is the bug we fixed in chapter one, turned into a rule so it stops being written in the first place.

beats.heading: The two rules
beats.narration: And the two rules that get broken most, marked important. Run the tests before claiming done. Never add a second lockfile. Both of those are things you just watched go wrong.

beats.heading: Twenty lines
beats.narration: Twenty lines to close four gaps. That is the best return on effort available anywhere in this tool.

segments.prompt: The same request as chapter four, now with the file in place

events.text: add a rate limiter to the login route

events.note: right manager, one lockfile
right directory, named export

beats.heading: Same words
beats.narration: Same project, same request, word for word. The only thing that changed is that twenty-line file is now sitting in the repository.

beats.heading: Byte for byte
beats.narration: Add a rate limiter to the login route. Identical prompt to the one that went wrong four minutes ago.

beats.heading: Right manager
beats.narration: pnpm this time, and one lockfile instead of two. It did not get smarter. It got told.

beats.heading: Right place
beats.narration: Right directory, named export, matching the file next to it. All three of those came from lines you can read in under a minute.

beats.heading: Green
beats.narration: And it ran the tests with the right command, unprompted, because the file told it to before saying a task was done. Forty-one passing.

beats.heading: The same prompt
beats.narration: The prompt did not get better. The context it runs inside did.

beats.heading: What is left
beats.narration: Now it knows the project. What it still does not have is a method.

segments.prompt: Chapter six card: the workflow

waypoint.promise: Explore, plan, code, commit — and why that order

beats.heading: Chapter six
beats.narration: It knows your project now. This chapter gives it a method, and the method is four words in a fixed order.

beats.heading: The order
beats.narration: Explore, plan, code, commit. Almost everyone starts at the third one, and that is the single most expensive habit in this whole video.

segments.prompt: Explore and plan: reading first, then a written plan with verification, then the approval gate

beats.heading: Plan mode
beats.narration: Plan mode. The important property is in the header. Nothing is edited until you approve, so everything that happens in the next ninety seconds is reversible by doing nothing.

beats.heading: Four words
beats.narration: The instruction has four words at the end doing all the work. Do not write code yet. Without them it starts editing, and you lose the chance to disagree cheaply.

beats.heading: Explore
beats.narration: So it explores instead. Two agents, forty-eight thousand tokens, reading how uploads already work here. This is the step people skip, and skipping it is what produces code that works but does not belong.

beats.heading: It is not free
beats.narration: That reading takes fifty-two seconds and eighteen thousand tokens, and it is the best money you will spend in the whole session. A plan built on a guess costs you an afternoon.

beats.heading: Changes by file
beats.narration: Then the plan, as a document you can argue with. Four files, and one of them marked no change needed. That line is the most reassuring thing in the list, because it means it considered the file and decided against touching it.

beats.heading: Verification
beats.narration: And this is the part that matters most, and the part a rushed session never writes. Five checks, each one something you could actually run. That list is what turns a plan into a contract you can hold it to.

beats.heading: The gate
beats.narration: Then the gate. Four answers, and they are not the same size. The first one hands over every edit for the rest of the session. The third keeps you in the loop on each one.

beats.heading: What to read
beats.narration: One habit to take from this chapter, and it is the most useful sentence in this video. Read the verification list before the file list. If those five checks are the wrong five, everything after this is wasted work, however good the code turns out to be.

beats.heading: The short step
beats.narration: Code is the step everyone thinks is the job. In a good session it is the shortest and least interesting part of the whole thing.

beats.heading: Against the contract
beats.narration: It works against the plan and then runs the tests itself, reporting them against the five checks it wrote earlier. Twenty-six lines folded away, because you do not need them unless something failed.

beats.heading: One more line
beats.narration: Then the move that costs one line and saves a bad merge. Ask a second agent to review what the first one wrote.

beats.heading: Fresh eyes
beats.narration: A reviewer with clean context is not attached to the plan. Two findings, one of them blocking, on code that passed every test.

beats.heading: The real bug
beats.narration: And it is a real one. The old avatar gets deleted before the new file is written, so if the conversion throws, the user loses the picture they already had. No test would have caught that.

beats.heading: Only then
beats.narration: Fixed, and only then committed. Four files, sixty-three lines, with a message that says what it did.

beats.heading: The order
beats.narration: Explore, plan, code, commit. The order is the technique, and the reviewer at the end is what makes the whole thing safe to run at speed.

segments.prompt: Chapter seven card: long sessions

waypoint.promise: Three controls for the budget from chapter three

beats.heading: Chapter seven
beats.narration: Remember that number in the corner from chapter three. This is the chapter where it runs out, and what to do when it does.

beats.heading: Three controls
beats.narration: Three controls. One buys back room, one undoes work rather than words, and one gives the session something to measure itself against.

beats.heading: Two hours in
beats.narration: Two hours in, forty-seven turns, and the number in the corner has been climbing the whole time. This is the state where most people quietly start getting worse results without noticing why.

beats.heading: Still working
beats.narration: It is still working, and it is still competent. Twenty-two thousand tokens read in that one step, which two hours ago would have been fine and right now is expensive.

beats.heading: Nearly full
beats.narration: Then the warning. Older turns are about to be summarised away, which means the instructions you gave it at the start are the first thing to go.

beats.heading: Buy back room
beats.narration: Compact is the first control. You type it on purpose, before you hit the wall, not after. It is not a restart and it does not end your session.

beats.heading: What survives
beats.narration: Forty-seven turns become fourteen bullets, and the context drops by an order of magnitude. What you were doing survives. The exact words you used getting there do not, and that is the trade.

beats.heading: The other one
beats.narration: Rewind is the second control, and it is the one almost nobody knows exists. Compact fixes running out of room. Rewind fixes going in the wrong direction.

beats.heading: How far back
beats.narration: It asks how far back, and what to bring with you. Code and conversation together, or one without the other. Restoring code only keeps everything you discussed and throws away what it wrote, which is stranger and more useful than it sounds.

beats.heading: Both on purpose
beats.narration: Use both of them deliberately. Compact before you hit the wall rather than after, and rewind instead of arguing with a session that has already drifted somewhere you did not want it to go.

segments.prompt: A standing goal the session measures itself against

events.text: /goal every route in src/routes has a test for its error case

events.note: it grades its own work now

events.text: All 14 routes now have an error-case test.

beats.heading: The third control
beats.narration: The third control is the one that changes how a long session behaves, rather than repairing it after the fact.

beats.heading: One sentence
beats.narration: You give it a standing goal. One sentence describing done, written before any code moves, and it stays pinned while everything else scrolls past.

beats.heading: It grades itself
beats.narration: Now it measures its own work against that sentence instead of against the last thing you happened to say. Nine of fourteen done, so it keeps going without being nudged.

beats.heading: Unattended
beats.narration: That is the difference in practice. You can look away for two minutes and come back to progress rather than to a question.

beats.heading: Finished
beats.narration: Fourteen of fourteen, fifty-five tests passing, and it stopped when the sentence was satisfied rather than when it ran out of ideas.

beats.heading: Still pinned
beats.narration: The marker in the corner is the point. The goal is still active, so the session always has something to be judged against.

beats.heading: Inside the repo
beats.narration: Everything so far has happened inside your repository. Now we let it out.

segments.prompt: Chapter eight card: MCP

waypoint.promise: Letting it read the systems your repository does not contain

beats.heading: Chapter eight
beats.narration: Half of what you need to answer a question at work is not in the repository. It is in the tracker, or the database, or the logs.

beats.heading: The gap
beats.narration: MCP is how it reaches those, and the name is the least interesting thing about it.

segments.prompt: How MCP works: your session, the client, a server, your systems, and back

nodes.label: You ask
nodes.note: a question about work, not code

nodes.label: Your systems
nodes.note: the tracker, the database, the logs

nodes.label: The answer
nodes.note: with the rows it actually read

beats.heading: Five parts
beats.narration: MCP is a protocol, and protocols always sound harder than they turn out to be. Five parts here, and the only piece that is new to you is the box in the middle of the row.

beats.heading: A work question
beats.narration: It starts with a question your repository cannot answer on its own. What is blocking this ticket. Which customers hit that error yesterday. Neither of those lives in your source code.

beats.heading: It picks a tool
beats.narration: It works out that answering means going outside the repo, and calls a tool instead of guessing. This is the same tool-calling you watched in chapter three, pointed somewhere new.

beats.heading: The server
beats.narration: The server is the only piece you install. One per system you want reachable, running on your machine, holding the credentials so the model never sees them.

beats.heading: A normal request
beats.narration: From there it is an ordinary API call to your tracker or a query against your database. Nothing exotic, and nothing the system on the other end treats differently.

beats.heading: It stays
beats.narration: The answer comes back and stays in context, so the next question builds on it rather than fetching it again.

beats.heading: The whole path
beats.narration: Ask, tool call, server, system, answer, and back into context. That is the whole of MCP, and the rest is which servers you choose to run.

events.note: a real read, not a recollection

events.text: postgres__query(select count(*) from avatars where url like '%.png')
It is blocked on the storage migration, and here is why that ordering is right.
lines: Converting on upload without migrating them leaves two formats live.

beats.heading: Two servers
beats.narration: Two servers connected in this session, the tracker and the database. The header tells you which ones, and it is worth a glance before you trust anything that follows.

beats.heading: A real question
beats.narration: The question is one you would actually ask a colleague, and no amount of reading the source code would answer it.

beats.heading: It reads the ticket
beats.narration: So it reads the actual ticket. Blocked, and blocked by a specific other ticket. That is a fact it fetched, not a plausible sentence it produced.

beats.heading: Then the database
beats.narration: Then it goes and counts. Forty-one thousand existing avatars still in the old format, which is the number that makes the blocking relationship make sense.

beats.heading: The real reason
beats.narration: And the answer explains the ordering rather than restating the ticket. Convert on upload without migrating the existing ones and you have two live formats in production.

beats.heading: Grounded
beats.narration: That is the real value. Not that it knows more, but that its answers are grounded in your systems rather than in something that sounds right.

segments.prompt: Chapter nine card: hooks

waypoint.promise: Turning a rule you asked for into one that is enforced

beats.heading: Chapter nine
beats.narration: Back in chapter five we wrote a rule. Run the tests before saying a task is done. It is a request, and requests get forgotten.

beats.heading: Enforced
beats.narration: Hooks turn that request into something the tool cannot skip.

segments.prompt: How a hook works: an event, a matcher, your command, and the exit code that decides

wiring.return: and the session is told why

beats.heading: A rule with teeth
beats.narration: A hook is a shell command that runs when something happens, and whose exit code gets to veto what just happened. Five parts in the row, and you own three of them.

beats.heading: It edits
beats.narration: It starts the moment the tool writes a file. Any write, in any session, whether you happened to be watching the screen at the time or not.

beats.heading: The event
beats.narration: That write fires an event before the result gets back to you, carrying which tool ran and which file it touched.

beats.heading: Your matcher
beats.narration: Your matcher decides whether you care. A pattern over the file path, so a hook on your source tree stays quiet when it edits a readme.

beats.heading: Your command
beats.narration: Then your command runs. A test suite, a linter, a formatter, a check that nobody has added a second lockfile to the repository. Anything your shell can do, you can enforce here.

beats.heading: And it hears why
beats.narration: A non-zero exit blocks the edit and the reason goes back into the session, so it knows what to fix rather than that something went wrong.

beats.heading: The whole hook
beats.narration: Edit, event, matcher, command, verdict. Deterministic every single time, whether the model remembered your rule or not.

segments.prompt: The hook fires and blocks an edit, enforcing the rule written in chapter five

events.note: three lines is a whole hook

events.text: add a burst allowance to the rate limiter

lines: ✗ 1 failing: rejects the 6th request in a minute
events.note: chapter five's rule, now enforced

events.text: The hook blocked that edit. The burst allowance broke the existing limit test.
lines: Fixing the test expectation first, then re-applying.

beats.heading: Three lines
beats.narration: Here is the whole hook. An event to listen for, a pattern to match, and a command to run. Three lines in a settings file that you commit with everything else.

beats.heading: What it says
beats.narration: After any write to a TypeScript file under source, run the test suite. That is the rule we wrote in prose in chapter five, now written where it cannot be skipped.

beats.heading: An ordinary ask
beats.narration: Then an ordinary request. Add a burst allowance to the rate limiter, which is exactly the sort of small change that slips through review.

beats.heading: It edits
beats.narration: Eight lines, and they look fine. This is the point where a session without a hook would tell you it was done.

beats.heading: Blocked
beats.narration: Instead the hook fires, the tests run, one fails, and the edit is rejected on a non-zero exit. Nobody asked it to check. It had no choice.

beats.heading: It hears why
beats.narration: And it gets told which test broke, so it fixes the cause rather than retrying blindly. That feedback is what makes a hook useful instead of merely strict.

beats.heading: Asked, then enforced
beats.narration: Chapter five asked for that rule. This chapter enforces it. That is the difference between a convention and a guarantee.

segments.prompt: Closing card: the arc complete, and what to do tomorrow

waypoint.promise: One thing to do before you write another prompt

beats.heading: All of it
beats.narration: That is the whole arc. One project, nine parts, and every part of it fixing something the part before it broke.

beats.heading: Tomorrow
beats.narration: If you do one thing tomorrow, do the fifth chapter. Run slash init in a real repository and cut what it writes down to twenty lines.

beats.heading: The order
beats.narration: Everything else on that list is easier once it knows where it is.

segments.prompt: Final card: write the file, then use the workflow

beats.heading: The one move
beats.narration: Almost every bad session in this video came from the same thing. It did not know where it was, and nobody had told it.

beats.heading: Then the method
beats.narration: So tell it once, in a file you commit. Then explore before planning, plan before coding, and let something else review before you push.
